user.name: 宝玉
user.description: AI Engineer, dedicated to learning and disseminating knowledge about AI, software engineering, and engineering management.

fullText:
推荐阅读：《用 Manus 改造 Manus，AI Native 组织改造的实践和思考》https://t.co/0MEN86K7ow 来自 Manus 很好的 AI Native 组织改造一手实践分享。

基于我的理解提炼一下要点：

【1】团队的工程基建，从对人友好，变成了向 AI 暴露接口

过去我们做工程基建，核心是提升开发者体验，怎么让工程师写代码更爽；但 AI 原生的第一性原理，是如何让 Agent 能接触到真实世界，自己能获得充足的上下文。

比如 Manus 把分散的仓库串成统一入口、让 AI 能在几秒钟内跑通端到端测试、给 AI 权限去读线上日志、看报警、发邮件、控制 Feature Flag，他们做的这些，都是在把整个软件开发生命周期和业务流彻底暴露给 Agent。

人能看到什么、操作什么，Agent 就必须能看到、能操作。当 Agent 能够自己可以验证结果，形成“修改-验证-排查”的闭环时，它才真正从副驾驶变成了司机。

【2】人和 AI 的交互，从过程控制微管理，变成了只给目标，要证据

在传统的模式里，人跟 AI 是结对的方式，AI 写一段人来修改，人还要操心上下文有没有超、代码写得优不优雅，是不是有垃圾代码。但实际上这种过程工程是低效的，就好比你作为一个管理者去微管理你的员工。

- 直接给结果
Manus 工程师把 Slack 里的需求原文一字不改丢给 Agent，老板要什么就告诉 Agent 要什么，不需要告诉 Agent 怎么做，Agent 自己会想办法完成任务。

- 要证据

当人不再一行行看代码时，怎么相信 AI 的结果是否靠谱呢？

Manus 用最好的模型做代码审核机器人，让 AI 自己证明自己做对了。Manus 让 Agent 用测试账号走完注册、支付流程并逐步录屏，产品经理看录屏就能指出哪里不对。

【3】AI 工作流，从人等 Agent，变成 Agent 等人

真正的 AI 原生工作流是高度异步、大规模并发的。如果你只有一个 Agent 在干活，你就得等着它干活，但如果你安排了很多 Agent 同时干活，那么你就不需要等，只需要频繁的在不同的 Agent 之间切换，要么在分配任务，要么验证下结果，效率可以很高。

Manus 的工程师一个人同时开着十几二十个 Session 处理需求；领导层把 20 多个待办丢给一个主控 Session，让它自己去拉取 Slack、Gmail 和 Notion 做背景调研并分发任务；市场部的数字 Agent 更是学会了只在一个工作台接收任务，把任务拆给后台的多个子 Session 并行跑，甚至通过定时唤醒在收到系统信号时自动干活，遇到工具不好用还能自己提需求改系统。

【4】组织极致扁平与敏捷，从以前明确的工种，到现在每个人都能身兼多职

传统软件工程里最大的损耗是在人和人之间。 前后端联调的扯皮、产品设计研发对文档理解的偏差、跨部门的排期与优先级错位，毕竟人类无法低成本地共享上下文，所以才不得不靠精细的分工来凑。

而当 AI 抹平了技术栈的鸿沟，分工就不再必要了。在 Manus，一个人可以写完前后端和移动端，7 个人维护 4 个 App；所有产品经理都提交过代码，甚至一半能独立上线功能。

当然这样做不是没有代价的，Manus 人均每月 1 万美元的夸张 Token 消耗，当然hidecloud 在文章中解释了：买的是时间和注意力。

买的是“消除人际沟通损耗”和“保护人类的注意力”。当很多事情不再需要找人问，不需要临时打断别人时，组织才真正实现了极致的扁平与敏捷。

【5】Agent 对话 Session 正在成为公司的新一代资产

对话流（Session / Thread）正在取代传统的文档和看板，成为组织的核心工作对象与记忆载体。组织的知识已经不依赖人和文档，还依赖于 Agent 是否能读得到。

Manus 的运维同事嫌总被找去帮忙发版，就把发版流程写进 Agents.md，之后谁都能让 AI 来发；同一项目的成员能看到彼此的 Session，不用再追着人问进度。

【6】当 AI 做了 90% 的事，人还剩下什么？

引用下 hidecloud 的话：
> 在 AI Native 组织里，人的角色没有变小，而是更集中了。定义问题，判断质量，决定什么值得做，并为结果负责。还有很重要的一点：与 AI 共同成长。

人的位置一直在往上移，从亲手做，到定规则、看证据、做决定。往上移的时候，要小心把判断也一起交出去。

执行可以交给 AI，思考要留给自己。

---

补充一个有意思的点，他们产品经理把需求用 AI 做成视频，然后把视频当需求文档提交，看了下他们的那个视频，确实这个功能要描述清楚不容易，配合视频会简单很多，这确实是一种降低人和人之间沟通损耗的办法。

其实可以试试 Claude Design，这种交互都也能描述清楚，绝大部分功能直接做成高精度原型比视频效果直观多了。

---

虽然现在各个团队都在喊 AI 原生转型，但要做好是真不容易，如果只是在传统流程上加上一点 AI，那很难真正做到 AI 原生。

真想要做好，可以学学 Manus 那样，一切围绕 Agent 重新建立分工和流程，还得舍得砸钱用最好的模型，现在这些模型虽然贵，但是一两年后 Fable 这样的模型成本可能也跟 DeepSeek Flash 差不多了。

GenAI Margins Can Easily Fall From 60% to 20%

The economics of GenAI is not just compute and energy. 

It’s also the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness. 

Note: I have a full podcast episode on this. Link below.

Point 1: GenAI products often look like software plus services.
 Gross margins of 60% can drop to 20% when you need humans keep the model correct.
 Retraining can take 100 to 1,000 times more compute than ongoing inference.

Point 2: The long tail can easily turn from a moat into a liability.
 TikTok won on niche demand, but niche AI answers often need humans in the loop.

It can be bad.

***Takeaways for Managers:

Takeaway 1: Set a target accuracy for each AI product and price the cost of being wrong.

Data Moats Are Overrated. Data Operations Are Not. 
I mostly do not believe in data moats. 

(More on this in my free weekly email, link below.)

Here is what I do believe in.

Data can make your operations much smarter and faster.

1.Customer insights are too easy to copy
 Amazon pairing two books is the kind of insight any rival can replicate.
 The real power is the right action for the right customer at the right moment in the right channel.

2. Fast, data driven decisions must be measured, not assumed.
 Jeff Bezos split decisions into reversible ones like pricing tweaks and irreversible ones like executive hiring.
 I track speed by counting the number and frequency of decision meetings.

3.Standardized data products are the key tool for agile teams.
 Ideally you have 50 to 100 agile teams working on features, pain points and new products.
 One data product with full customer behavior can serve many teams for years.

***Takeaways for Managers:

→ Ask each manager to name one current assumption and the data that would prove it.

fullText:
I see how some people can watch flashy robot demos on the timeline and think with a shiver that the robot apocalypse is around the corner, but reality check:

There is no robot in the world that can change the batteries in a jack-o-lantern.

If you have a robot friendly door handle it might be able to walk outside, pick it up, and carry it back inside. The robot could open the drawer with your batteries in it, but then things get tough.

Opening the package of AA batteries?
Extracting a precision screwdriver from its case?
Unscrewing four tiny screws that require a hard press and twist?
Popping batteries out of the case?

Yes, you could build and train a specialist robot to do that today, but there is a very long way to go to replace the full range of human capabilities. Near term doomer scenarios should stop at “secretly controlling humanity” instead of “wiping humanity out” 😀

fullText:
This is an incredible moment in this history of mathematics, computer science, physics & science with some of the hardest problems in human history being solved by AI over a period of weeks. Depending on your perspective, it's either a crisis, a triumph, or both. I don't think anyone knows for sure. We're all trying to make sense of it. I oscillate between fear/dread and optimism/excitement on a daily basis. The rate of progress is insane, including today's announcement from OpenAI of more problems solved.

To help make sense of all of it, here's my conversation with three mathematicians about this moment. Each of them is an expert in the field of each of the biggest problems solved: Navier-Stokes, quasi-Riemann hypothesis, the unique games conjecture and complexity theory more generally.

Ankur Moitra is a mathematician and theoretical computer scientist at MIT, visiting the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. Steven Brunton (@eigensteve) is a mathematician and fluid dynamics expert at UW. Alex Kontorovich (@AlexKontorovich) is a mathematician at Rutgers specializing in number theory.
